sketches.title: Fake Sommelier
sketches.premise: The host pours a familiar non-wine drink and gives both players the same two-word tasting card. Write one lush tasting note that makes the card’s two nouns feel like they belong together in the glass. The host explains why your note is gloriously overconfident, then awards points for how far it stretches before it stops being a tasting note.
sketches.criterion: The note must describe the drink’s taste, smell, texture, or finish as if it were a wine, while keeping both card nouns meaningfully present.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence of tasting-note prose using both nouns; for example, card **banana + thunder**: “A soft banana nose opens into thunder on the finish, with a loud, buttery aftertaste that refuses to leave.”

sketches.title: Pairing Disaster
sketches.premise: The host names a non-wine drink and deals two ordinary nouns that supposedly describe its perfect pairing. Each player writes a tasting-note headline selling that pairing to a skeptical table. The host applauds the culinary crime, scores the strongest connection, and gently asks who invited this bullshit to dinner.
sketches.criterion: The headline must keep both nouns as recognizable parts of one plausible food-or-drink pairing claim.
sketches.move_shape: Write a short headline and optional one-sentence blurb using both nouns; for example, card **sock + honey**: “Sock & Honey: a chewy, floral pairing for people who have lost a bet.”

sketches.title: Finish the Glass
sketches.premise: The host serves a non-wine drink and gives both players the same tasting-note sentence with two blank spots marked by two nouns. Fill the blanks so the sentence becomes a vivid, funny note without breaking its shape. Points reward the biggest leap from plain drink description to memorable nonsense that still works.
sketches.criterion: Your completion must preserve the sentence’s tasting-note grammar and make both supplied nouns function as the two required images.
sketches.move_shape: Complete one sentence with both nouns in order; for example, card **moon + socks**: “On the finish, it leaves a taste of moon and warm socks, somehow cleaner than that sounds.”

sketches.title: Blind-Tasting Alibi
sketches.premise: The host gives both players a non-wine drink plus two nouns, then asks for a tasting note that secretly hints at a real, checkable fact about the drink without saying the fact outright. After both notes are read, each player guesses which note contains the better hidden clue. Points go to notes that remain deliciously vague while still pointing somewhere real.
sketches.criterion: The note must use both nouns and imply a true fact about the named drink without directly naming or contradicting that fact.
sketches.move_shape: Write one coded tasting note; for example, card **cola + airplane** and drink **cola**: “Dark, fizzy, and built for a long journey, with cola sweetness lifting like an airplane at takeoff.”

sketches.title: Notes from the Wrong Bottle
sketches.premise: The host names a non-wine drink and deals two nouns that do not belong in its usual description. Turn them into a confident tasting note, as though the bottle has just revealed a shocking new side. The host scores the note for preserving the drink’s identity while dragging the two outsiders into the glass by their shoelaces.
sketches.criterion: The note must still identify the named drink through sensory details while giving both nouns a clear sensory role rather than merely mentioning them.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence that anchors the drink and transforms both nouns into sensations; for example, drink **hot chocolate**, card **garage + lemon**: “Thick hot chocolate with a garage-dark roast and a sharp lemon spark cutting through the cream.”

sketches.title: Last Sip Roast
sketches.premise: The host pours a non-wine drink and gives both players two everyday nouns. Write a tasting note that praises the drink while sneaking in a roast of the person who would order it. The host checks that the note remains a real sensory description, then pays extra for a savage little finish that still lands on the tongue.
sketches.criterion: The note must describe the drink through taste, smell, texture, or finish, keep both nouns active, and make the insult target the drinker rather than replace the tasting note.
sketches.move_shape: Write one affectionate but cutting tasting note; for example, card **pillow + shark**: “Soft as a pillow, with a shark’s cheap bite on the finish—perfect for anyone who calls beige a personality.”
